lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.quote: The amounts, in pesos, spent by $5$ customers are $20,22,25,26,300$. Find the mean and median. Which one better shows a typical amount for this data set?
lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.note: Example #6 now makes the student compute both centers and justify why the median better represents the clustered values with an outlier.

lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.quote: A larger weight gives that value more effect on the result. A **weighted mean** uses the weights instead of counting every listed value equally.
lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.note: Core Concept now explains the weighting principle and why a larger weight changes how much a value influences the average.

lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.quote: The median mainly depends on the order of the values. One extreme value may change a lot without moving the median much.
lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.note: The abstract “exact magnitude” wording was replaced with two short concrete sentences about order and an extreme value.

lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.quote: For nearby numbers, you can compare each value with an easy middle number.
lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.note: The shortcut now uses plain wording about an easy middle number and immediately defines deviation before listing the differences.
The weighted-mean formula and weighting principle now appear in Core Concept before Example #5 applies them.

lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.quote: In set (b), $2$ and $3$ each appear $2$ times, which is the highest frequency. The modes are $2$ and $3$.
lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.note: Example #3 now includes a tied-highest-frequency data set and explicitly identifies both values as modes.

lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.quote: The best measure depends on the data. The mean uses every value, so one very large or very small value can pull it away from most of the data.
lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.note: The former four-sentence paragraph has been split into shorter paragraphs, each staying within the one-to-three-sentence limit.

lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.quote: A **weight** tells how much a value counts in an average.
lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.note: Weight and weighted mean are now defined in Core Concept before the weighted-grade example uses subject units as weights.

lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.quote: A **deviation** here means how far a value is above or below that chosen number.
lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.note: Deviation is now defined immediately before the shortcut lists positive and negative deviations from the chosen middle number.

lesson-statistics-and-probability-measur.quote: A **mode** is a value that appears most often.
